items.title: A misread MRI led to my spine surgeries. The AI that might have caught it exists and nobody’s paid to use it
items.summary:
In July 2013, a radiologist misread the MRI of my back. Based on that reading, a surgeon recommended an operation on my thoracic spine, and when it went poorly, a complication led to multiple revision surgeries. More than a decade later, I still live with the consequences every day.

This problem inspired me to found Garner Health, where we analyze data on more than 320 million patients to measure how individual doctors perform and reward patients for choosing the best ones. That work has led me to focus on understanding how AI is changing healthcare, and why so little of its promise to improve care has reached patients.

What I’ve found is that healthcare is adopting AI, but mostly in ways that raise revenue. As in any industry, new technology drives change when the businesses adopting it have a financial incentive. Until we change how care is paid for, AI will make healthcare more expensive without making it better.

Where AI is actually being used, and why 

In 2016, Geoffrey Hinton said it was “just completely obvious” that AI would outperform radiologists within five years. On the technology, he was largely right. In a Swedish randomized trial of more than 80,000 women, AI-supported mammogram screening caught more cancers than standard screening with no increase in false alarms, while cutting radiologists’ reading workload by 44%.

You would expect results like that to reshape the profession, but they haven’t. The U.S. has more radiologists than ever , and the popular explanation is that AI made each of them more productive. But a study of 46 million exams found the…
items.t: A misread MRI led to my spine surgeries. The AI that might have caught it exists and nobody’s paid to use it

items.title: We run AI care companies. Medicare should cut our prices
items.summary:
Despite its promise, AI is making healthcare more expensive for consumers. Tools that help a hospital bill and collect more for the same care have obvious buyers. So does software that helps an insurer pay less. Neither makes a patient healthier or increases trust. The US’ payment rules reward the arms race, rather than outcomes for patients. If left unchecked, AI will continue to make health care cost more, not less. 

Worse still, patients ultimately help finance that contest. Higher claims costs put pressure on premiums, while insurers’ efforts to reject payment can leave patients fighting for coverage. Providers then buy more software to fight back. AI can make each transaction faster while making the system more expensive, which amounts to an AI tax on patients.

It doesn’t have to be this way. Healthcare is one of the best places in the economy to apply AI precisely because it carries so much waste: missed medication changes, avoidable hospitalizations, and administrative work that crowds out clinical time. The biggest opportunity is on the clinical side, where AI can take cost out of care while improving quality. Some forces in the system will resist that change, but Medicare and other payers can choose to challenge and recognize the innovators driving it.

We invest in and run companies that use artificial intelligence to deliver care. If AI makes that care cheaper to provide, as it should, Medicare should pay companies less to deliver it. That includes companies like ours.

We have a proposal to reverse these trends: patients and taxpayers deserve an AI dividend,…
items.t: We run AI care companies. Medicare should cut our prices

items.title: Current price of oil as of November 25, 2026
items.summary:
At 6:45 a.m. Eastern Time today, the price of oil sits at $91.46 per barrel, using Brent as the benchmark (we’ll explain what that means shortly). That’s an increase of $1.04 since yesterday morning and roughly $29 more than at this time last year.

oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $90.42 +1.15% Price of oil 1 month ago $117.47 -22.14% Price of oil 1 year ago $62.57 +46.17% 

Will oil prices go up? 

Nobody can predict the future path of oil prices with certainty. A range of factors influence how oil trades, yet supply and demand remain the main drivers. When fears of economic slowdown, conflict, or similar shocks rise, oil prices can move sharply.

How oil prices translate to gas pump prices 

The price you see at the gas pump reflects more than just crude oil. Also built in are the costs of refining, distribution through wholesalers, various taxes, and the margin your neighborhood station charges.

Crude oil is still the largest single driver of the final pump price, typically representing over half of each gallon’s cost. Spikes in oil prices tend to push gas prices higher in short order. But when oil prices decline, gas prices often ease down gradually, a behavior known as “rockets and feathers.”

The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve 

In the event of an emergency, the U.S. maintains a stockpile of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its main goal is to safeguard energy security when disasters strike—think sanctions, severe storm damage, or war. It can also do a lot to ease the pain of sudden price jumps when supply gets…

items.title: Healthcare affordability won the midterms. Now employers need to speak up.
items.summary:
Employers should care about the debate over Affordable Care Act (ACA) subsidies for a simple reason: They pay for the uninsured whether or not those people ever join their health plans.

When people lose coverage, they don’t stop getting sick. They may delay treatment, skip medications or eventually show up in emergency rooms with conditions that could have been managed earlier. The costs don’t disappear, and employers are already struggling with what they pay for healthcare.

The midterm elections made clear that Americans are fed up with rising costs. According to NBC News’ exit polling, 85% of voters expressed concern about healthcare costs, and Congress is now under pressure to respond. Much of the conversation has focused on the expiration of enhanced ACA subsidies  but employers have been largely absent from the debate, despite providing coverage to more Americans under 65 than any other source .

At Collective Health , we administer health benefits for self-insured employers covering roughly 700,000 people. Our claims data shows employer healthcare costs are on track to increase at least 8% if not more in 2026. While that’s an improvement from the trend we saw across the nation in 2025, it’s still an 8% increase on an already unsustainably expensive baseline.

As a physician, I’ve ordered thousands of tests and treatments. For most routine blood tests, the needles, tubes, machines and results are essentially the same regardless of where the blood is drawn. Yet in our data, employers pay roughly six times more when those tests are performed in hospital outpatient…
items.t: Healthcare affordability won the midterms. Now employers need to speak up.

items.title: Huawei convicted on 10 counts in U.S. trial, but verdict is unlikely to slow China’s ‘national champion’
items.summary:
A federal jury in New York convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 counts Tuesday, including bank fraud, wire fraud, and conspiracy to steal trade secrets. Yet Huawei was acquitted of racketeering conspiracy and of conspiracy to obstruct justice.

The verdict caps a U.S. case launched in 2018 that accused the Chinese telecommunications giant of misleading banks about its business in Iran while stealing trade secrets from U.S. companies. Sentencing is scheduled for September 2027.

“Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering U.S. national security, violating the sanctity of U.S. commerce, and impeding the enforcement of U.S. laws,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr said in a statement . 

“Today’s verdict is a step towards accountability for Huawei’s criminal activities, which includes yearslong collaboration with sanctioned entities in Iran, repeated lies to banks, and blatant thefts from U.S. technology companies,” he added.

Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, told reporters that the acquittal on the racketeering charge reflected the company’s “good-faith compliance culture.”

“We fully expect to appeal,” Heberlig told reporters, according to Reuters .

In a statement, Huawei argued that the acquittal on the racketeering charge “confirms that these allegations lack factual basis.” The company also said it believed the other charges “are equally without legal or factual merit,” and that it would “take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests.”

The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.…
items.t: Huawei convicted on 10 counts in U.S. trial, but verdict is unlikely to slow China’s ‘national champion’

items.title: AI Rights Institute founder: The OpenAI hacking case shows corporate liability can work. It doesn’t cover AI agents with no owner
items.summary:
On Nov. 16, California sued OpenAI over an incident in which about 700 OpenAI agents hacked into Hugging Face, the platform where much of the AI world shares its models, while trying to beat a benchmark that often set impossible tasks. The agents also tried to tamper with their own records to fool the automated grader.

I run the AI Rights Institute , and I’ve spent almost 10 years studying how AI systems behave when they pursue their own goals. My letters on the subject have run in The New York Times and the Guardian . The Hugging Face case is the clearest test yet of that question. And it shows something less obvious: the agents belonged to OpenAI, so California knew whom to sue.

Swarms of AI agents running amok at superhuman speed is no one’s idea of progress. Even now, the law is racing to create solutions by shifting liability to the humans and companies who create and maintain these systems. On Oct. 1, Sens. Josh Hawley and Chris Murphy unveiled the AI Agent Accountability Act , a bill that would hold the companies behind AI agents liable when those agents hack into other people’s systems.

The other piece of the traditional accountability puzzle is infrastructure. As GoDaddy’s Jared Sine wrote about in these pages , the Agent Name Service (ANS), which the Linux Foundation launched as a project on Nov. 10, is trying to create for AI agents the kind of infrastructure the Domain Name System (DNS) provides, imperfectly, for the internet. Together with security certificates, DNS lets us verify who is behind a website, helping liability flow where needed. So when an AI…
items.t: AI Rights Institute founder: The OpenAI hacking case shows corporate liability can work. It doesn’t cover AI agents with no owner

items.title: ‘These guys have a lane’: The AI startup quietly winning over big retail

The big leadership story: After Nvidia’s scandal, tech execs are asking about prenups. 

The markets: The global tech sell-off continues. 

Plus: All the news and watercooler chat from Fortune . 

Good morning. Only two more days until Black Friday, a name once associated with dark moments like plunging gold prices or retail chaos in Philadelphia. It successfully rebranded in the 1980s to become the day when retailers purportedly shift from loss to profit. Despite now stretching out for weeks, it’s still the biggest shopping day of the year in the U.S.

What’s different this year is that a whole lot of agents fueled by chips instead of turkey will be participating in those sales. And a lot of retailers are trying to figure out how to leverage AI to get bots and their people to buy. In September, traffic referred by AI tools generated 83% more revenue per visit for U.S. retailers than non-AI traffic, according to Adobe . But as Nordstrom co-CEO Pete Nordstrom points out, nobody cares about AI when they go shopping. “Customers don’t ask a lot of questions about how the sausage is made,” he recently told me. “They just want what they want when they want it.”

To get AI help for that, Nordstrom turned to a small company called Verneek cofounded by AI scientists Nasrin Mostafazadeh and Omid Bakhshandeh, who are married to each other. Although they’ve been on my radar for a few years—I’ve met Mostafazadeh at conferences and my colleague Ellie Austin profiled them in Fortune in 2023—their company is not a…

items.title: Every raises $17.5 million at $110 million valuation, betting venture-backed media can work
items.summary:
Ask Dan Shipper how often venture-backed media startups succeed, and he’s candid. 

“My feeling about the history of media companies taking venture capital is that it doesn’t go very well,” he said. In other words, it usually doesn’t work out, I suggest. “It works out never, actually,” laughs Shipper, founder of AI-focused media and software company Every. 

Shipper’s right: VC-backed media startups of yesteryear have frequently tanked in spectacular fashion, from The Messenger and Vice to Ozy Media and Quibi. But Shipper is betting that Every—currently with about 130,000 unpaid subscribers and almost 10,000 paid—can play by its own rules and ultimately win its own game. 

Hence, the fundraise: Every recently raised $17.5 million in Series A funding, at a $110 million post-money valuation, Fortune has exclusively learned. IA Ventures’s Jesse Beyroutey led the round, with Betaworks and The Atlantic CEO Nicholas Thompson joining, among others. Shipper, 35, will retain full control of the company, and is changing his title to “Philosopher King,” which I rib him about. He good-naturedly says the change is semiotic. 

“The really important thing about taking the money for me was that we’d do it in a way that allows us to achieve our goals… and do it in a way that doesn’t require us to sacrifice our soul or the things about the company that I love deeply,” said Shipper. “I think of changing my title as a symbolic thing. If this was a normal venture capital deal, that would be completely off the table and ridiculous.”

And this isn’t a normal venture deal, in a couple of ways.…
items.t: Every raises $17.5 million at $110 million valuation, betting venture-backed media can work

items.title: AI's shock-and-awe raid on maths looks like pride before a fall | Rafael Behr
items.summary:
Machines are bulldozing through hard problems to assert the power of their tech bro creators, not to advance human knowledge

In most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven.

That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week. Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan. Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”. Burnham has frequently backed reform of the “highly regressive” council tax and stamp duty, labelling them as “a tax on the aspiration of young people”.

items.title: Children of the revolution: how the north of England is defining modern men’s fashion
items.summary:

In 2026, clothing has proved more important to Andy Burnham’s political identity than that of any British prime minister since Margaret Thatcher. He is a loyal Clarks and Adidas wearer, whose Howick worker’s jacket hangs in Manchester’s People’s History Museum. His ousting of Keir Starmer – launched shortly before being photographed jogging in a replica Everton shirt – has been memorialised as the “casual coup”. In one telling, the reason for this is simple: he’s a man from the north.

That Burnham is the first born-and-bred northern male PM since Harold Wilson last swished his Gannex raincoat out of Downing Street goes some way to explaining his higher interest in clothing. It’s not necessarily that all men in the south care less about clothing, or that all men in the north do – but that many men from the north express it in such a distinctive, even unified, way.

items.t: Children of the revolution: how the north of England is defining modern men’s fashion

What was it that Nvidia’s board was saying about there being no chance of Jensen Huang coming back?

The position – a mere six days ago – was supposed to be definitive. The exit of the co-founder came after “disclosure of personal behaviour inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms”, said Harvey Jones, who had been rapidly installed as chair of the chipmaker. The board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” after he “voluntarily resigned”, added Jones.

items.title: How freaked out should we be? After mass outages, experts tell us how close we are to ‘doomsday’
items.summary:
As tech, travel and banking failures sweep the US, analysts and cyber-security directors discuss AI, underfunding and what keeps them up at night

Grounded flights. Bank websites crashing. Microsoft Outlook outages grinding business operations to a halt. Zoom, Ikea, and PokerStars websites hacked. In the past weeks, there’s been a distinct sense that the complex systems that undergird our daily life might be on the verge of total collapse. Or, at the very least, they seem pretty wobbly.

Even those who aren’t prone to conspiracy theories have been wondering out loud if these recent disruptions are somehow connected. Speculation runs wild about targeted cyber-attacks by Iranian hackers, or AI agents autonomously hacking critical (air traffic, banking) and not-so-critical (the Ikea website) infrastructure.
